newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Court threat as Swiss find few Mobutu millions.
newsitem.headline: Court threat as Swiss find few Mobutu millions.

text.p: Switzerland's secretive banks have found only $3.4 million in toppled Zairean ruler Mobutu Sese Seko's assets, including shares, securities and a safe deposit box, banking watchdogs said on Tuesday.

The sum, a fraction of the billions Kinshasa says Mobutu has stashed away here, was immediately disputed by a fierce government critic who predicted a long legal wrangle over the deposed dictator's controversial fortune.

The Federal Banking Commission (FBC), which last month ordered all 406 Swiss banks to report any Mobutu riches they might hold, said six banks had found 4.8 million Swiss francs ($3.4 million) in assets owned by Mobutu, his family or their associates.

Berne froze Mobutu's assets -- including a 30-room, $5.5 million luxury mansion -- after he was toppled in May by rebels, whose leader Laurent Kabila took over as president of the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo.
FBC deputy director Daniel Zuberbuehler said the commission considered the matter closed, although he said returning the funds to Kinshasa could take years under Swiss legal procedures.
"As the banking supervisor, basically we are satisfied. I don't think we can order any other search. I think we have done more than anyone else in the world," Zuberbuehler told Reuters.
The Commission did not name the banks holding Mobutu funds. But Zuberbuehler said the bulk of the money, more than four million Swiss francs, was at one bank in two "fat accounts".
The rest of the assets were in smaller accounts. One was dormant and had seen no movement for more than 20 years.
Zuberbuehler said a safe deposit box had also been found but added: "You wouldn't have big amounts of assets in a safe deposit box."

In a newspaper interview last week, new Kinshasa Justice Minister Celestin Lwangi alleged Mobutu had 11 billion Swiss francs ($7.7 billion) here. But Zuberbuehler dismissed what he called wild stories.
"There are no billions. Of course they can say anything but these would be dreams. It would be nice if Mobutu had billions here, but he probably has spent the money."

Socialist member of parliament Jean Ziegler said Swiss banks held $4 billion in assets of Mobutu, who, according to French pilots he once employed, used to send his private jet from Kinshasa to France just to buy fresh croissants and groceries.
"This is grotesque," Ziegler told Reuters. "Swiss banks lied once again to defend their client Mobutu."
Ziegler, a member of a commission set up by Kinshasa's Geneva representatives to trace Mobutu's wealth abroad, said he would do his utmost to ensure justice was done.
He said former rebels had shown him evidence including bank documents uncovered at Mobutu's jungle palace in Gbadolite.
"There are bank transfer orders from Kinshasa to Zurich. They found in his Gbadolite palace passbooks, codewords and a lot of information on numbered Swiss bank accounts," he said.
"Now the only way we have is to go to court. The Zaireans will nominate lawyers here and they will start a court battle."
Critics suspect the worst of Swiss banks, which were swept up in protracted scandals over the Swiss assets of such toppled dictators as the former Philippine leader Ferdinand Marcos.
Another scandal is the last thing Switzerland needs when its image has been damaged by charges that its banks hoarded the wealth of Jews murdered by Hitler in World War Two.
Under Swiss law, Kinshasa would have to file criminal proceedings at home against Mobutu in order to have a case here.
The Swiss government, in response to a request from Zairean officials, has also demanded that anyone else -- including financial managers -- report assets of Mobutu they hold.
Silvia Matile-Steiner, spokeswoman for the Swiss Bankers Association, said nothing had been announced under that order.
The tiny Alpine principality of Liechtenstein said it had found no evidence so far that Mobutu had accounts in its banks, but added it wanted more information from Kinshasa. ($ = 1.429 Swiss Francs)
